method_card.title: Tally Charts, Tabulation and Pictograms
method_card.content:
A tally chart is a quick way to count items as they occur. Each item is recorded with a vertical stroke; the fifth stroke is drawn diagonally across the previous four to form a bundle of five, making counting fast and accurate. Always group your tally marks into fives before reading totals.

A frequency table organises data into categories with their corresponding frequencies. When data is numerical, it is grouped into class intervals — for example, “10 ≤ h < 20”. Each interval uses ≤ on the left and < on the right so that no value falls in two classes at once.

A pictogram uses a repeated symbol to represent data. The most important step is reading the key carefully: if one symbol represents 4 items, then half a symbol represents 2 items. The most common Foundation error is ignoring the key and treating every symbol as worth 1.

When critiquing a diagram, look for: a truncated axis (y-axis not starting at zero), an incorrect scale (unequal gaps), and distorted sizing (symbols at different sizes). Any of these can mislead the reader about differences in the data.

When choosing formats: use a tally chart to collect live data; a frequency table to present data clearly; a pictogram when frequencies are whole multiples of the key value.
steps: Read the key on any pictogram before counting symbols
Multiply the number of complete symbols by the key value
For partial symbols, use the fraction shown (half symbol = half the key value)
Check a frequency table by summing all frequencies to get the total
Identify misrepresentation by checking whether the axis starts at zero and the scale is even
State why the misrepresentation is misleading, not just that it exists

exam_context.marks: 1–4 marks per question; pictogram reading is typically 1–2 marks, table completion up to 4 marks
exam_context.frequency: At least one tally/table/pictogram question appears on every paper; pictogram key errors are the single most common Foundation 1-mark drop

worked_examples.question: A pictogram shows the number of books read by students in a week. The key states: one symbol = 4 books. One student’s row shows 3 complete symbols and one half symbol. How many books did that student read?

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the key
steps.content: Each complete symbol = 4 books. A half symbol = 2 books.

steps.label: Step 2 — Count and multiply
steps.content: 3 complete symbols: \(3 \times 4 = 12\) books. Half symbol: \(0.5 \times 4 = 2\) books.

worked_examples.question: A frequency table shows the scores of 40 students on a quiz: Score 1–10: 8 students; Score 11–20: 14 students; Score 21–30: frequency missing; Score 31–40: 7 students. Find the missing frequency.

A bar chart showing monthly rainfall has its y-axis starting at 20 mm rather than 0 mm. The bar for June reaches 30 mm and the bar for July reaches 60 mm. A student claims July had three times as much rainfall as June. Explain whether this is correct.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read the true values
steps.content: Both bars must be read from zero. June = 30 mm; July = 60 mm.

steps.label: Step 2 — Calculate the true ratio
steps.content: \(\frac{60}{30} = 2\). July had twice as much rainfall, not three times.

steps.label: Step 3 — Explain the misrepresentation
steps.content: The truncated axis makes the bar for July appear three times the height of June on the chart, but the actual values show only a two-fold difference.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The student is wrong. The truncated axis exaggerates the visual difference. The true rainfall ratio is 2:1, not 3:1.

bronze.display: A pictogram uses one football to represent 6 goals. A team’s row shows 4 complete footballs. How many goals did the team score?

misconceptions.message: Read the key first: 1 symbol = 6 goals. 4 symbols = 4 × 6 = 24 goals. Do not count each symbol as 1.

bronze.display: A pictogram uses one apple to represent 8 items. A row shows 2 complete apples and one half apple. How many items does this represent?

misconceptions.message: 2 complete = 2 × 8 = 16. Half apple = 0.5 × 8 = 4. Total = 16 + 4 = 20.
Don’t forget to include the half symbol: it represents half the key value, which is 4 here.

bronze.display: A tally chart records five-mark bundles. Three bundles and two extra strokes are shown. How many items are recorded in total?

misconceptions.message: 3 bundles of 5 = 15. Plus 2 extra strokes = 17. Count the diagonal stroke as the 5th mark in a bundle, not an extra.

bronze.display: A frequency table has four categories with frequencies 12, 9, 15, and 4. What is the total frequency?

misconceptions.message: Add all frequencies: 12 + 9 + 15 + 4 = 40.

bronze.display: A pictogram shows 3 complete symbols and one quarter symbol. The key is: 1 symbol = 20 items. How many items does this row represent?

misconceptions.message: 3 × 20 = 60. A quarter symbol = 0.25 × 20 = 5. Total = 60 + 5 = 65.

bronze.display: In a grouped frequency table for heights, which class interval correctly includes the value 150 cm?

misconceptions.message: Standard class intervals use ≤ on the left and < on the right. 150 satisfies 150 ≤ h < 160 (it is the left boundary of this class).

bronze.display: A frequency table shows 5 classes with frequencies 3, 7, 11, 8, and 1. Which frequency value corresponds to the modal class?

misconceptions.message: The modal class is the one with the highest frequency. Here that is 11.

bronze.display: A frequency table for favourite sports has 5 rows with a total of 60. Four rows show frequencies 18, 12, 9, and 14. What is the fifth frequency?

misconceptions.message: Sum the known: 18 + 12 + 9 + 14 = 53. Missing = 60 − 53 = 7.

silver.display: A pictogram for daily visitors uses the key: 1 symbol = 50 visitors. Monday: 3 symbols; Tuesday: 4.5 symbols; Wednesday: 2 symbols; Thursday: 3.5 symbols. How many more visitors came on Tuesday than on Wednesday?

misconceptions.message: Tuesday: 4.5 × 50 = 225. Wednesday: 2 × 50 = 100. Difference = 225 − 100 = 125.
Apply the key to both rows before subtracting. Don’t subtract symbol counts first.

silver.display: A grouped frequency table for journey times shows: 0–10 min: 6; 10–20 min: 18; 20–30 min: f; 30–40 min: 9. The total is 50. Find f.
A bar chart has its y-axis starting at 50 instead of 0. Group A bar reaches 80 and Group B bar reaches 100. A reporter claims Group B scored twice as many as Group A. Select the best response.
options: Yes, the bar for B is visually taller
No, the true values are 80 and 100, a ratio of 4:5
Yes, because 100 is double 50
No, both groups scored the same

misconceptions.message: True values are read from zero: 80 and 100. Ratio = 80:100 = 4:5, not 1:2. The truncated axis creates a visual illusion.

silver.display: A pictogram for rainfall uses: 1 raindrop = 5 mm. A month shows 7 complete raindrops. A second month has 45 mm of rainfall. How many complete symbols should be drawn for the second month?

misconceptions.message: Number of symbols = 45 ÷ 5 = 9. Check the value is an exact multiple of the key.

silver.display: Which of these is NOT an example of graphical misrepresentation?
options: A bar chart with the y-axis starting at 30 rather than 0
A pictogram where each symbol represents a different number in different rows
A frequency table listing every class interval with equal width
A chart where the bars for larger categories are drawn physically wider

misconceptions.message: A frequency table with equal-width classes is correctly constructed. Options A, B and D all describe recognised forms of misrepresentation.

silver.display: A tally chart records shoe sizes of 30 students. Frequencies: size 5: 4; size 6: 9; size 7: 10; size 8: f; size 9: 2. Find f.

gold.display: A pictogram shows monthly sales using two different keys: Product A key = 200 units per symbol, Product B key = 400 units per symbol. Product A shows 3.5 symbols; Product B shows 2.25 symbols. How many more units did Product B sell than Product A?

misconceptions.message: Product A: 3.5 × 200 = 700. Product B: 2.25 × 400 = 900. Product B sold 900 − 700 = 200 more units. Apply the correct key to each product row.

gold.display: A grouped frequency table for exam scores has classes 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80 with frequencies 2, 8, 22, 18. Which statement correctly explains why a pictogram would NOT suit this data?
options: Pictograms can only show up to 4 categories
Frequencies like 22 and 18 are not easy multiples of a simple key value, making symbols hard to draw accurately
Pictograms cannot show grouped numerical data at all
The total frequency of 50 is too large for a pictogram

misconceptions.message: Pictograms work best when frequencies are whole multiples of the key. The format justification must refer to the data’s numerical properties.

gold.display: A frequency table for phone call durations (minutes) shows classes 0–5, 5–10, 10–15, 15–20 with frequencies 14, 26, 19, 11 (total 70). The original tally had a total of 72. In which class is a tally error of 2 most likely?
options: 0–5 (frequency 14)
5–10 (frequency 26)
10–15 (frequency 19)
15–20 (frequency 11)

misconceptions.message: The shortfall of 2 could occur in any class, but the class with the most tally bundles (frequency 26, i.e. 5 full bundles plus 1) has the most opportunity for a miscounting error.

gold.display: A pictogram uses symbols of different sizes: routes with more passengers have larger symbols. Each symbol still represents the same number. Does this pictogram have a misrepresentation error?
options: No misrepresentation — as long as the key is constant, symbol size doesn’t matter
Yes — varying symbol sizes create distorted sizing, misleading readers about relative frequencies
Yes — pictograms must use exactly 10 symbols per row
No — larger symbols just make the chart easier to read

misconceptions.message: Distorted sizing is a recognised form of misrepresentation. Even if the key is constant, varying symbol sizes cause readers to perceive area differences rather than count differences.

gold.display: A frequency table records goals scored per match over 38 matches: 0 goals: 8; 1 goal: 12; 2 goals: 9; 3 goals: 6; 4 or more goals: 3. What fraction of matches saw the team score at least 2 goals? Give your answer in its simplest form.

misconceptions.message: At least 2 goals: 9 + 6 + 3 = 18 matches. Total = 38. Fraction = 18/38 = 9/19.
Include the ‘4 or more’ row — ‘at least 2’ includes all classes from 2 onwards.
